title: Why does water boil sooner up a mountain?
hook: At 2,300 meters above sea level, water boils at about 92 °C, and beans take longer to cook.
summary: With less air pressure, water boils at lower temperatures: it boils sooner but cooks more slowly.
cardText: Up high, there’s less air pressing on the water, so it boils at a lower temperature: about 92 °C at 2,300 meters. It boils sooner but cooks more slowly.

cardBlocks.text: At sea level, water boils at 100 °C. At about 2,300 meters above sea level (7,500 feet), water boils at around 92 °C. The reason is air pressure.

Boiling means steam bubbles forming inside the liquid, and that only happens once the water’s vapor pressure matches the pressure of the air above it. High up, there is less air pressing down, so this happens at a lower temperature. The result: water boils sooner but cooks more slowly, because it never gets as hot. Beans, for example, take much longer to soften.
Lower air pressure means a lower boiling point: water boils sooner but cooks more slowly.

deepDiveBlocks.text: A pressure cooker does the opposite

A pressure cooker traps steam and raises the pressure inside. With more pressure, water only boils above 100 °C, typically near 120 °C. Those extra 20 degrees cut cooking times substantially. Embrapa lists a pressure cooker as one option for preparing biofortified common beans.

At the top of Mount Everest, nearly 8,850 meters up, water boils at roughly 70 °C, too cool to hard-boil an egg. However long you wait, the white never firms up completely: its main protein needs about 80 °C to set. The yolk does set.
High-altitude baking recipes often adjust ingredients and oven temperature, because liquids evaporate faster and leavening behaves differently.

claims.text: Water boils when the vapor pressure in its bubbles matches the pressure of the air above it.

support.excerpt: The boiling point is the temperature at which the vapor pressure of a liquid is equal to the external pressure.
When the vapor pressure inside the bubbles is equal to the external atmospheric pressure, the bubbles rise to the surface of the liquid and burst.

claims.text: With less air pressure at high altitude, water boils at a lower temperature.

support.excerpt: As atmospheric pressure decreases, water boils at lower temperatures.
Because atmospheric pressure can change based on location, the boiling point of a liquid changes with the external pressure.

claims.text: Because the boiling water is cooler, food cooked in it takes longer; beans, for example, take longer to cook at altitude.

support.excerpt: Because water boils at a lower temperature at higher elevations, foods that are prepared by boiling or simmering will cook at a lower temperature, and it will take longer to cook.
